analysis.one_liner: Would have let pesticide makers delay EPA action on pesticide residue limits by requiring more data first.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees, EPA sent an unfavorable review in July 1999, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1996 Congress told the EPA to re-examine the legal limits on pesticide residues left on food, using tougher safety standards, and to revoke limits that proved unsafe. This bill would have slowed that process: the EPA could not lower or revoke a residue limit until it had collected and considered new data supporting the pesticide's continued use, deadlines for re-reviewing old limits would become optional, and emergency-use pesticide approvals would be easier. It also ordered reports on how pesticide rules affect U.S. farm exports. It died in committee without a single hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Pesticide manufacturers, whose products would stay on the market longer because the EPA could not revoke a residue tolerance until new data was gathered and weighed. Farmers and food processors would keep access to crop-protection tools the 1996 law might have removed, and growers would find it easier to get emergency-use pesticide approvals. The EPA itself would gain flexibility, since review deadlines would apply only when the agency decided it was in the public interest.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA could not modify, suspend, or revoke an existing pesticide residue limit until it had obtained and considered additional data supporting that limit's continuation, which would delay removals from the market.

The deadlines in current law for re-reviewing thousands of older pesticide tolerances would apply only when the EPA Administrator determined it was in the public interest, effectively making the schedule optional.

The EPA could issue tolerances for emergency pesticide uses without first re-examining the pesticide's other residue limits, speeding up approvals growers request when they face pest outbreaks or trade disruptions.

Before finalizing rules on residue limits, the EPA would have to publish proposed rules with 60-day comment periods and advance notices, giving pesticide producers and agricultural interests more opportunities to weigh in before decisions take effect.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost through longer exposure to pesticide residues reviewed under the older, less protective framework, because limits found potentially unsafe would stay in effect while new data was collected. The EPA's food-safety re-review would slow down, since staff time would shift to gathering data before acting. The bill itself acknowledged the 1996 law's process was designed to remove exposures found to exceed safe levels.

drawbacks.text: The bill's central data requirement would have kept tolerances in effect even when the EPA had already determined there may be grounds for revoking them, delaying action on residues the agency suspected exceeded safe levels.

The bill's backers had a real argument: the 1996 law set ambitious review deadlines based on new scientific concepts like cumulative and aggregate exposure that the EPA had never used before, and required data that did not yet exist. Acting on worst-case assumptions before better data arrived could have disrupted agriculture and removed useful pest-control products without clear health gains.

The bill required new EPA and Agriculture Department reports on funding needs and international competitiveness but provided no money, leaving agencies to absorb the reporting workload from existing budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — making sure the EPA's decisions rest on complete data rather than worst-case assumptions — was a fair criticism of a rushed implementation schedule, and the bill's findings are specific about it. But the mechanism it chose cuts the other way: by barring the EPA from acting until new data was collected, it would have delayed the removal of residue limits the agency already suspected were unsafe, and the burden of that delay would fall on the public's food, not on the industry seeking the delay.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Commerce and Agriculture Committees, then to two subcommittees, where it stayed; EPA sent an unfavorable written review in July 1999, no hearing or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ray LaHood introduced the bill on March 25, 1999, and it was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the House Agriculture Committee.

In mid-April 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Agriculture Subcommittee on Department Operations, Oversight, Nutrition and Forestry, and the agencies were asked for their comments.
On July 15, 1999, the House received an unfavorable executive comment from the EPA on the bill.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired with the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and food-safety enforcement came out ahead: because the bill died, the EPA kept its authority under the 1996 law to tighten and revoke pesticide residue limits on its existing schedule. Pesticide makers and growers did not get the added delays and flexibility the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food-safety rules; pesticide makers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Ray LaHood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FQPA Implementation Act of 1999 in the House.

for.name: 15 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: House Commerce and Agriculture Committees
against.role: Committees of referral; their subcommittees never held a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees in April 1999 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Environmental Protection Agency
against.role: Federal agency that would administer the pesticide residue program
against.what_they_did: Delivered an unfavorable executive comment on the bill to the House in July 1999.

sides.party_line_note: Fifteen of the sixteen cosponsors were Republicans and one was a Democrat; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would have let their products keep selling under residue limits the EPA already had grounds to revoke, until new supporting data was gathered. Their gain is the public's continued exposure to residues under old safety reviews.

Farmers would keep access to crop-protection chemicals the 1996 law might have withdrawn, and emergency-use approvals would come faster. Some of that access comes at the cost of residue limits that consumers eat under.

Slower tolerance revocations would keep ingredients and treated commodities on the market that might otherwise lose their legal residue limits, avoiding disruption to supply chains. The cost shows up as residue exposure for consumers.
